body:
Understanding Prehistoric Gujarat

Prehistory refers to the period of human existence before written records became available. Knowledge of prehistoric communities comes mainly from the objects and remains they left behind, including stone tools, animal bones, human burials, pottery and traces of habitation.

Gujarat has a long prehistoric past. Stone tools found in its river valleys demonstrate the presence of early human communities, while the sandy plains of North Gujarat preserve important evidence of later hunter-gatherers. Sites such as Langhnaj and Loteshwar help explain how people obtained food and adapted to the environment before and during the gradual emergence of farming and herding.

Prehistoric Gujarat was not occupied by one uniform culture. Different communities lived in river valleys, grasslands, sandy plains and coastal regions. Their tools and food habits varied according to local resources and the period in which they lived.

The 3 Main Stages of the Stone Age

Palaeolithic: Old Stone Age

The Palaeolithic Age was the earliest and longest stage of the Stone Age. People depended mainly on hunting wild animals, gathering edible plants and using naturally available resources. Stone tools included handaxes, cleavers, choppers, flakes and scrapers. Different types of tools were used in different phases of the Palaeolithic.

The Palaeolithic is commonly divided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases. In Gujarat, Palaeolithic tools have been reported from several river valleys and adjoining uplands, including parts of eastern Gujarat.

Mesolithic: Middle Stone Age

The Mesolithic Age is especially important for understanding prehistoric North Gujarat. Its characteristic stone tools are microliths, meaning small, carefully shaped stone implements. Many were fitted into wooden or bone handles to make larger tools or weapons.

Mesolithic communities continued hunting, gathering and fishing. Some groups occupied places near water sources repeatedly or for extended periods. The remains from Langhnaj demonstrate this way of life particularly well.

Neolithic: New Stone Age

The Neolithic Age is associated with developments such as polished stone tools, cultivation of plants, domestication of animals and more permanent settlements. These developments gradually changed how people obtained and stored food.

However, the transition to food production did not occur everywhere at the same time. Some communities continued hunting and gathering even after farming and herding had developed in neighbouring regions.

A Basic Chronological Framework

For introductory Indian history, NCERT provides the following broad chronological framework:

  • Palaeolithic: From approximately 2 million years ago to about 12,000 years ago.
  • Mesolithic: Approximately 12,000 to 10,000 years ago in the introductory textbook framework.
  • Neolithic: Beginning around 10,000 years ago, with substantial regional variation.

Chronological qualification

These dates describe a broad educational sequence, not fixed boundaries for every archaeological culture. In Gujarat, microlith-using hunter-gatherer communities survived well beyond the introductory Mesolithic date range. Some existed during periods when farming, herding and metal use were already present elsewhere.

Why Stone Tools Are Important

Stone tools provide evidence of human activity because they often survive long after wood, cloth and other materials have decayed. Their forms reveal the kinds of work early people performed.

  • Handaxes and cleavers: Larger tools associated particularly with the Lower Palaeolithic.
  • Flakes and scrapers: Implements used for activities such as cutting and scraping.
  • Microliths: Small tools especially characteristic of Mesolithic technology, commonly used in composite implements.
  • Polished stone implements: Commonly associated with Neolithic communities, including tools used for cutting and working wood.

Tool types help distinguish prehistoric cultures, but a single tool does not always establish an exact date or prove a particular occupation. Older technologies sometimes continued alongside newer ones.

Prelims focus

  • Prehistory concerns human societies before the availability of written records.
  • Palaeolithic means Old Stone Age.
  • Mesolithic means Middle Stone Age and is especially associated with microliths.
  • Neolithic means New Stone Age and is associated with developments in food production and polished stone tools.
  • Langhnaj is an important Mesolithic site in Gujarat.
  • Trap: The appearance of agriculture did not immediately end hunting and gathering throughout India.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, printed pp. 11–20, and Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, pp. 22–29; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, 2012, Chapter 1, Prehistoric Rock Paintings, printed pp. 1–4; Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, section Microlithic Settlements, pp. 328–329, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Prehistoric Gujarat: The Stone Age and Its Main Stages

body:
Why the Environment Mattered

Prehistoric people depended directly on their surroundings for food, water, shelter and materials for making tools. Gujarat contains several contrasting physical regions, so communities living in different areas encountered different opportunities and difficulties.

Rivers provided water and attracted animals. Grasslands supported grazing animals. Forests supplied edible fruits, roots and other plant products. Rocky areas provided material for making tools. The availability of these resources influenced where people lived and how frequently they moved.

Eastern Gujarat: Rivers, Hills and Stone Tools

Eastern Gujarat contains rocky uplands and river valleys connected with the Aravalli and Vindhyan hill systems. The Mahi and Narmada river systems, together with valleys such as the Orsang and Sukhi, form an important geographical setting for prehistoric occupation.

Water, wild vegetation, animals and stone resources made parts of this region suitable for early human communities. Palaeolithic remains from eastern Gujarat demonstrate that the state's prehistoric history began long before the Mesolithic occupation represented at Langhnaj.

Important Palaeolithic evidence has been reported from the Orsang region and from places such as Jogpura in the Sukhi valley and Bhuvera in the Panam valley. The remains include older stone-tool industries, including Middle Palaeolithic assemblages.

Eastern Gujarat: Remember the connection between river valleys, rocky resources and Palaeolithic evidence. Langhnaj represents a different, better-known Mesolithic setting in the sandy plains of North Gujarat.

North Gujarat: Sandy Plains and Seasonal Water

North Gujarat has relatively dry plains, areas of grassland and numerous old sand dunes. Rivers associated with the region include the Sabarmati, Banas and Rupen. Rainfall varies, and many smaller watercourses depend strongly on the monsoon.

Between sand dunes, low-lying depressions can collect rainwater. Such water bodies provided drinking water for people and animals. Grass and shrubs supported herbivores, including antelope and deer, which were important food resources for prehistoric hunters.

Langhnaj is situated in this broader environmental setting. Its evidence demonstrates that prehistoric communities used landscapes containing sandy rises, vegetation and accessible water rather than relying only on permanent riverbanks.

The environment was not identical to the present-day landscape. Climatic conditions changed over thousands of years, and archaeological animal remains indicate that some species occupied areas where they are uncommon today.

Saurashtra and the Coastal Region

Saurashtra contains rocky terrain, river valleys and a long coastline. Rivers such as the Bhadar and Hiran have yielded evidence relevant to Gujarat's prehistoric record.

The coastline and nearby inland environments offered different resources from those of North Gujarat's sandy plains. Marine and coastal food resources could supplement the resources available inland. However, the precise food habits of a particular prehistoric community must be understood from its own evidence rather than assumed from its proximity to the sea.

Why Hunter-Gatherers Moved

Hunter-gatherers obtained food mainly from wild plants and animals instead of depending primarily on cultivated crops and domesticated livestock.

Their food could include edible roots, fruits, nuts, seeds, birds, fish and wild mammals. Knowledge of seasonal changes was essential because different resources became available at different times.

Movement between locations occurred for several connected reasons:

  • Food availability: A frequently used area might no longer provide sufficient food.
  • Animal movement: Hunters could follow animals moving between grazing areas and water sources.
  • Seasonal plants: Different fruits, seeds and other edible plants became available in different seasons.
  • Water supply: Seasonal pools and streams could dry up, requiring movement to another source.

Mobility did not necessarily mean continuous wandering. A group might return to a favourable campsite season after season or remain there while local resources were sufficient.

Stone Tools and Daily Activities

Early people used stone tools for cutting, scraping, processing plant materials and preparing animal products. Some tools were attached to handles made from wood or bone.

In Mesolithic communities, microliths made effective cutting points or edges when fitted into a larger implement. Common forms included small blades, points, triangles, trapezes and crescents, also called lunates.

Microliths are particularly useful for identifying the technological traditions of hunter-gatherer communities in North Gujarat. However, they should not be interpreted as proof that every person using them had exactly the same diet or settlement pattern.

Environmental Change and Food Resources

Around 12,000 years ago, the world experienced major climatic changes associated with the end of the last Ice Age. Relatively warmer conditions encouraged the spread of grasslands in many regions.

Grasslands provided food for grazing animals such as deer, antelope, sheep, goats and cattle. People who hunted these animals became familiar with their movements and habits. Such knowledge may have contributed to the eventual development of herding in some regions.

Wild grain-bearing grasses also became important food resources. Collecting these plants was different from deliberately cultivating them, but familiarity with their growth and seasonal cycles helped create conditions in which farming could eventually develop.

Prelims focus

  • Eastern Gujarat has important Palaeolithic evidence associated with river valleys and rocky uplands.
  • The Orsang and Sukhi valleys are associated with prehistoric stone-tool evidence.
  • North Gujarat contains sandy plains and dune landscapes used by Mesolithic communities.
  • Seasonal water sources attracted humans and wild animals.
  • Microliths include small blades, points, triangles, trapezes and crescents.
  • Trap: Hunter-gatherers could repeatedly occupy the same location; their way of life did not require continuous movement.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, printed pp. 11–18; Gopesh Jha, Vidhi Kothari, Varun Vyas and P. Ajithprasad, Assessing Systematic Blade Production in the Indian Subcontinent with Special Reference to Eastern Gujarat, Quaternary 6(2), 2023, article 25, section 3.1, Research Area, consulted 17 November 2026; Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, section The Environment of Gujarat, pp. 325–327, consulted 17 November 2026; IGNOU, Indian Mesolithic Cultures, Unit 2, sections 2.2 and 2.5, printed pp. 18–22, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gujarat’s rocky eastern valleys, northern sandy plains and Saurashtra coast offered different resources and supported different prehistoric occupations.
pictures.caption: How Gujarat's different landscapes provided resources for prehistoric communities.

title: Gujarat's Prehistoric Environment and the Life of Hunter-Gatherers

body:
Location and Historical Importance

Langhnaj is an important prehistoric site in the present-day Mehsana district of Gujarat. It is especially associated with Mesolithic hunter-gatherer communities and the use of microlithic stone tools.

The site lies within the sandy plains of North Gujarat, where ancient dunes and nearby depressions formed a landscape capable of supporting people, plants and wild animals.

Langhnaj is significant because the remains include not only stone tools but also animal bones, human skeletal remains and other objects associated with daily life. These different kinds of evidence provide a fuller picture of its prehistoric inhabitants.

Langhnaj — Mehsana district — Mesolithic culture — microliths, animal remains and human skeletons.

Excavations and Important Contributors

The archaeologist H. D. Sankalia conducted major investigations and excavations at Langhnaj during the 1940s, including work between 1941 and 1949.

Irawati Karve, an anthropologist, and G. M. Kurulkar, an anatomist, also contributed to the investigation of the human skeletal remains.

The association of Langhnaj with H. D. Sankalia is an important historical fact. His excavations helped establish the importance of the microlith-using prehistoric communities of Gujarat.

Evidence of Stone-Tool Technology

A major category of evidence from Langhnaj consists of microliths and other stone implements.

Microliths are small pieces of worked stone that could serve as cutting edges, points or parts of larger implements. Crescent-shaped microliths, known as lunates, are especially associated with the microlithic tradition of the Sabarmati region.

Such tools were useful for hunting and processing materials. They could form part of arrows, spears or cutting implements when attached to suitable handles.

The presence of larger stone implements alongside microliths is not surprising. Mesolithic communities could use both small composite tools and other stone implements according to their needs.

Animal Remains and the Food Economy

Animal remains found at Langhnaj provide important evidence about the fauna of prehistoric North Gujarat and the resources used by its inhabitants.

Reported animal remains include species such as:

  • Rhinoceros
  • Wild boar
  • Spotted deer and other deer
  • Nilgai
  • Blackbuck

The remains of wild animals are consistent with an economy in which hunting played an important role. Evidence of aquatic resources also supports the importance of fishing and the use of nearby water bodies.

The rhinoceros remains are especially notable because they indicate the presence of a large wild animal in the prehistoric landscape. They should not be taken to mean that the present environment of Mehsana is identical to the environment in which these animals lived.

Plant foods probably supplemented meat and fish. Grinding stones and related implements indicate that plant materials could be processed, although such implements alone do not prove that the users cultivated crops.

Human Remains and Burial Practices

Langhnaj is also notable for the discovery of human skeletal remains. Historical excavation reports describe several skeletons, including remains found in flexed positions, meaning that parts of the body were bent rather than fully extended.

These findings demonstrate that human remains formed an important part of the archaeological evidence at the site.

Human burials do not automatically establish that a community lived permanently in one place or depended on farming. The evidence must be understood together with its tools, food remains and broader settlement context.

Other Objects Found at Langhnaj

Excavations also yielded objects such as grinding implements, beads, pottery fragments and metal objects from the deposits investigated at the site.

These finds are important because microlithic technology was used over a long period, including times when pottery and metal objects were present in parts of Gujarat.

Do not confuse different kinds of evidence

Finding microliths together with pottery or metal objects in a site's archaeological record does not prove that all the objects were manufactured at the same time or used by a single, exclusively farming community. Langhnaj is best remembered for its Mesolithic or microlithic tradition, while the later materials require chronological distinction.

What Langhnaj Reveals About Prehistoric Gujarat

Langhnaj shows that prehistoric North Gujarat supported communities familiar with its dry plains, seasonal water sources and wild animals.

Its inhabitants used small stone implements, exploited wild food resources and occupied a landscape that provided water and vegetation. The combination of tools, animal remains and human skeletons makes it one of Gujarat's best-known prehistoric sites.

Prelims focus

  • Langhnaj is located in Mehsana district, Gujarat.
  • It is especially associated with Mesolithic and microlithic culture.
  • H. D. Sankalia conducted important excavations at Langhnaj during the 1940s.
  • Irawati Karve contributed to the study of the human remains.
  • The finds include microliths, human skeletons and animal remains, including rhinoceros.
  • Trap: Langhnaj is not principally identified as a Harappan city or as an early agricultural village.

[Sources: IGNOU, Indian Mesolithic Cultures, Unit 2, section 2.5, Langhnaj, printed pp. 21–22, consulted 17 November 2026; Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, section Microlithic Settlements, printed pp. 328–329, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, published archaeological account of Gujarat prehistory reproduced in the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts ASI document collection, discussion of the Langhnaj excavations; Rhino Resource Center, bibliographic record and summary of H. D. Sankalia and Irawati Karve, Early Primitive Microlithic Culture and People of Gujarat, American Anthropologist 51(1), 1949, pp. 28–34, consulted 17 November 2026.]
